viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
@BLKMDL3 @wholemars In case anyone is curious:

We’ve had a ~pixel-perfect world model since last year, which is critical for synthetic data generation. 

The (much) smaller version of that in the car is a conditional mean-flow model, based on the recent sequence of Tesla Universal Vision Encoder features, which are the same ones that are plugged into the 3B encoder model that produces the driving actions. 

We fork off from these UVE features, then run a separate ~1B diffusion model. This takes in the previous reality-view generation with added noise and then denoises it to the current visualization. 

It then produces a small video chunk (8 images at 36 fps, at the resolution of the UI screen). This work is done by 1/2 of a TRIP engine every UVE frame at 18 hz and is spread over 4 cycles. 

Currently, the latency is a bit high due to compute constraints, but we have ways to interleave newer UVE features along the diffusion transformer layers to cut roughly 35% of the latency.
viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_zh:
@BLKMDL3 @wholemars 如果有人好奇：

自去年以来，我们已经有了一个像素完美的世界模型，这对于合成数据的生成至关重要。

汽车中的（小得多）版本是条件平均流模型，基于 Tesla 通用视觉编码器功能的最新序列，这些功能与插入到产生驾驶动作的 3B 编码器模型中的功能相同。

我们从这些 UVE 功能中分叉出来，然后运行一个单独的 ~1B 扩散模型。这会吸收先前生成的添加了噪声的现实视图，然后将其降噪到当前的可视化中。

然后它会生成一个小视频块（8 个图像，36 fps，UI 屏幕的分辨率）。这项工作由 TRIP 引擎在 18 Hz 的每个 UVE 帧上完成，并分布在 4 个周期内。

目前，由于计算限制，延迟有点高，但我们有办法沿着扩散转换器层交错更新的 UVE 功能，以减少大约 35% 的延迟。

viral_ticker_tweets.full_text_en:
T3 Code founder just shared his personal setup for building agentic teams with Grok Bot + Opus 5.5

one Grok Bot runs your whole fleet of machines. Opus 5.5 does the coding. you only approve

how:

→ Grok Bot gets one MCP link to T3 Code
→ you give it one rule: code goes to Opus 5.5
→ it spins up threads on every machine you own
→ works from your phone, even with the laptop closed

save the video, here's the guide:

• step 0 → what it is:

Grok Bot = always-on agent with its own cloud computer

T3 Code = open-source control plane for coding agents. free, runs on your machines, uses your subscriptions

• step 1 → the stack:

- Claude $100 plan → Opus 5.5 for the actual code
- Grok Bot → the dispatcher that never sleeps
- T3 Code on every box you want it to control

• step 2 → connect the fleet:

run npx t3 connect on each machine. one command, free, no Tailscale needed

• step 3 → give Grok Bot the keys:

Settings → Environments → Copy MCP URL → paste it into Grok Bot, sign in with OAuth. it can now see every linked machine

• step 4 → the one rule Theo uses:

tell Grok Bot "call T3 Code with Opus 5.5 for any task where it is applicable"

code runs on your Claude plan, Grok Bot's limits stay free for planning

• step 5 → make it work:

- "spin up an Opus 5.5 thread on each machine to check disk & RAM"
- "go through these PRs and pick the best ones"
- "split the backlog, one thread per issue, each in its own worktree"

every thread gets its own branch. nothing merges without your approval

what to expect:
- 8 threads on 8 machines from one chat (Theo's demo)
- works over the internet, not computer use
- control everything from your phone
- T3 Code: $0. you pay for Claude + Grok Bot only

honest take:

this is a dispatcher, not magic. bad briefs still give bad PRs, and you still review every diff. the win: your agents keep working while you're away from the desk

Save it so you don't lose it. 

then read the full guide on building AI agent teams in T3 Code in the article below ↓

T3 Code 创始人刚刚分享了他使用 Grok Bot + Opus 5.5 构建代理团队的个人设置

一个 Grok Bot 可以运行您的整个机器群。 Opus 5.5 负责编码。你只认可

如何：

→ Grok Bot 获得一个指向 T3 代码的 MCP 链接
→ 你给它一条规则：代码转到 Opus 5.5
→ 它会在你拥有的每台机器上旋转线程
→ 即使笔记本电脑关闭，也可以通过手机工作

保存视频，这是指南：

• 步骤 0 → 它是什么：

Grok Bot = 拥有自己的云计算机的永远在线代理

T3 Code = 用于编码代理的开源控制平面。免费，在您的计算机上运行，​​使用您的订阅

• 步骤1 → 堆栈：

- Claude 100 美元计划 → Opus 5.5 的实际代码
- Grok Bot → 不眠的调度员
- 您希望它控制的每个盒子上都有 T3 代码

• 步骤2 → 连接车队：

在每台计算机上运行 npx t3 connect。一个命令，免费，无需 Tailscale

• 步骤 3 → 给 Grok Bot 密钥：

设置 → 环境 → 复制 MCP URL → 将其粘贴到 Grok Bot，使用 OAuth 登录。它现在可以看到每台链接的机器

• 步骤 4 → Theo 使用的一条规则：

告诉 Grok Bot“使用 Opus 5.5 调用 T3 代码来执行任何适用的任务”

代码在您的 Claude 计划上运行，Grok Bot 的限制对计划保持免费

• 步骤 5 → 使其发挥作用：

- “在每台机器上启动 Opus 5.5 线程来检查磁盘和 RAM”
-“浏览这些 PR 并选择最好的”
- “拆分待办事项，每个问题一个线程，每个线程都在自己的工作树中”

每个线程都有自己的分支。未经您的批准，任何内容都不会合并

期待什么：
- 8 台机器上的 8 个线程通过一次聊天（Theo 的演示）
- 通过互联网工作，而不是使用计算机
- 通过手机控制一切
- T3 代码：0 美元。您只需支付 Claude + Grok Bot 的费用

诚实地采取：

这是调度员，不是魔法。糟糕的内裤仍然会带来糟糕的公关，而你仍然会审查每一个差异。胜利：当您离开办公桌时，您的座席仍能继续工作

保存它，以免丢失。

paragraphs: BILL Holdings BILL has entered into a definitive agreement to be acquired by TPG, Inc. TPG, a global alternative asset management firm, in partnership with Corpay, Inc. CPAY. The all-cash transaction values BILL at approximately $6 billion, with shareholders set to receive $63.25 per share. The offer represents a 31% premium to BILL's 60-day volume-weighted average share price as of Nov. 16, 2026.

Under the agreement, TPG will acquire a majority interest in BILL through TPG Capital, the firm's U.S. and European private equity platform, while Corpay will acquire a minority stake. The partnership brings together TPG's technology investment and business-building experience with Corpay's expertise in payments and spend management. The companies aim to strengthen BILL's financial operations platform and expand its capabilities for small and midsize businesses.

The transaction was unanimously approved by BILL's board and is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals. The deal has no financing conditions attached. Following completion, BILL will become a privately held company and will no longer trade on a public stock exchange.

BILL's recent financial performance provides further context for the acquisition. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, total revenues increased 13% year over year to $353.8 million, while core revenue grew 14% to $316.4 million. The company served 475,300 businesses and processed $102 billion in payment volume, up 14% year over year. Non-GAAP operating income more than doubled to $136.9 million, reflecting improved operating efficiency.

BILL's integrated platform, growing payment volumes and improving profitability provide a solid foundation for future growth. The TPG-Corpay partnership could provide additional resources and expertise to support product innovation, AI development and long-term growth.

top_three.summary_en: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei defended their $900 billion AI infrastructure commitments ahead of their IPO, emphasizing a balanced approach between rapid growth and responsible AI development. The founders reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining an atypical organizational culture while scaling computing resources.
paragraphs: Two years before she pulled off the largest public offering of all time, Daniela Amodei gathered everyone at Anthropic in a 16-acre garden on a sweltering fall day near the Santa Cruz mountains.

The AI company now with a market value of roughly $1.18 trillion was at the time still a young startup that Amodei and her big brother, Dario, had co-founded with five friends. It was undergoing a hiring spree and Daniela was worried. So they carted 10-foot-tall bookshelves onto the grass to make reading nooks, played games and made friendship bracelets. As the company’s president, and keeper of its culture, the younger Amodei wanted to deliver a message.
“Keep Anthropic weird,” Daniela told them.

Anthropic embraces being atypical because it believes the artificial intelligence future will be anything but normal. Many co-founders meet in college, or at a first job. This pair met when he was 4 and she was born.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei have defended the artificial intelligence (AI) company's massive infrastructure commitments and reiterated their focus on responsible AI development, saying its record-breaking initial public offering (IPO) will not change its long-term mission.

Speaking to CNBC International ahead of Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, the siblings addressed the company's $900 billion AI commitments, its approach to balancing growth with safety, partnerships with major technology companies and its relationship with the US government.
Daniela Amodei described the IPO as a significant milestone but said the company would remain focused on its original objectives.

Addressing questions around Anthropic's substantial AI infrastructure spending, Dario Amodei defended commitments of around $900 billion, arguing that they should be viewed in the context of the company's cash reserves and growing revenue.
Amodei added that Anthropic tries to "err on the low side" when forecasting its computing requirements.
He also acknowledged the challenge of balancing the pace of AI development with safety considerations, describing it as one of the company's central tensions.

"What we've done with pacing is essentially said, look, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour. Spend time figuring out how to do that safely, and the rest of that surplus we spend building the model in the right way," he said.
On the expectations surrounding Anthropic's public market debut, Amodei said the company was keeping its focus on execution rather than the spotlight.

fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】Dario Amodei（CEO），Daniela Amodei（总裁）在纳斯达克上市前夕访谈：回应9000亿美元基建投入并强调安全开发与企业文化一致性
【起因与机理】应对资本市场对其高昂资本开支及商业化压力的质疑
【关键数据与实测】关键细节：明确9000亿美元支出规模，并强调采用“90英里/小时”而非“200英里/小时”的开发节奏。
【行业影响与走向】行业影响：该高额资本开支将持续推高行业进入门槛，重塑大模型初创企业的资本运作范式。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Dario Amodei (CEO), Daniela Amodei (President) (Pre-IPO media briefing): Defense of $900B infrastructure spending and commitment to safety-first development
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Addressing market concerns over heavy capital expenditure and commercial pressures
[Key Metrics] Specific details: $900 billion in committed spend, adopting a '90 mph vs 200 mph' development pace strategy.
[Industry Impact & Outlook] Industry impact: Massive CAPEX requirements are shifting the capital model for AI startups, raising entry barriers.

topic_focus.title_zh: 英伟达芯片走私深陷间谍调查，前CEO黄仁勋面临国会听证
topic_focus.title_en: Nvidia Chip Smuggling Scandal Leads to Spy Probe and Congressional Hearing
topic_focus.summary_zh: 美情报机构证实英伟达前CEO黄仁勋的绯闻对象爱丽丝·黄卷入通过复杂空壳网络向中国输送高端AI芯片的走私案。财长贝森特已介入，要求彻底核查英伟达对华合规销售责任，黄仁勋将于12月1日出席国会闭门听证会，涉及高端算力流向的违规链条正被全面起底。
topic_focus.summary_en: Intelligence agencies confirmed that Alice Huang, associate of ex-CEO Jensen Huang, managed a smuggling network channeling Nvidia chips to China. Treasury Secretary Bessent has demanded a full audit of Nvidia's compliance, with Jensen Huang scheduled for a closed-door Congressional hearing on December 1st, exposing massive cracks in chip export controls.

perspective_pro.speaker_zh: 美国财政部及情报委员会
perspective_pro.point_zh: 必须切断高端芯片对华流向，任何私下的商业利益输送均被视为危及国家核心安全，对违规行为的零容忍是维护芯片主导权的唯一手段。
perspective_pro.point_en: Cutting off high-end compute to China is a national security imperative; private profit channels cannot supersede state-level containment strategies to maintain technological supremacy.

perspective_con.speaker_zh: 跨国芯片分销商与供应链专家
perspective_con.point_zh: 全球化贸易体系错综复杂，过度单一的制裁只会催生更多地下走私网络，导致合规成本激增，却无法改变算力市场供需严重不平衡的现实。
perspective_con.point_en: The complex global trade architecture makes total isolation impossible; heavy-handed sanctions only push the industry into black-market shadows, ballooning compliance costs without solving the fundamental supply-demand mismatch.

topic_focus.title_zh: 斯坦福数学家完成黎曼猜想形式化证明
topic_focus.title_en: Stanford Mathematician Levent Alpöge Completes Formal Proof of Riemann Hypothesis
topic_focus.summary_zh: 斯坦福数学家勒文特·阿尔珀格通过1700万行Lean代码，完成了对数学皇冠明珠——黎曼猜想的证明，并获得Mathlib社区官方认证。此事件标志着数学证明进入了“形式化验证时代”，即通过AI辅助和计算机语言消除人类逻辑推演的漏洞。
topic_focus.summary_en: Stanford mathematician Levent Alpöge has formally proven the Riemann Hypothesis using 17 million lines of Lean code, officially verified by the Mathlib community. This milestone signals the dawn of the 'formal verification era' in mathematics, leveraging machine-checked logic to eliminate human error.

perspective_pro.point_zh: 传统人类审稿机制已无法应对高度复杂的现代数学，Lean等机器证明语言能提供100%的逻辑可靠性，是科学发现的未来。
perspective_pro.point_en: Human-based peer review can no longer handle the complexity of modern math; languages like Lean provide 100% logical reliability, representing the definitive future of mathematical discovery.

perspective_con.speaker_zh: 基础数学界资深理论家
perspective_con.point_zh: 过分依赖机器验证可能剥夺数学的直觉美感。如果证明本身无法被人类直观理解，那么这种逻辑符号的堆砌是否失去了数学研究的本质意义？
perspective_con.point_en: Over-reliance on machine verification may strip math of its intuitive elegance; if a proof remains incomprehensible to human thought, the essence of mathematical exploration is compromised.

topic_focus.title_zh: AI编程智能体实测任务成功率不足一成
topic_focus.title_en: AI Coding Agents Show Less Than 10% Success Rate in Real-world Simulation
topic_focus.summary_zh: 最新研究显示，尽管AI编程智能体在SWE-bench测试中表现卓越，但在模拟真实工作环境的集成项目协作中，任务完成率却不足10%。与此同时，多家银行因合规与安全风险封禁第三方AI代理，揭示了实验室高分与生产环境低产的巨大落差。
topic_focus.summary_en: Recent research reveals that while AI coding agents shine on benchmarks like SWE-bench, they complete fewer than 10% of tasks in integrated workplace simulations. Simultaneously, major banks are banning AI agents due to security risks, highlighting a massive gap between lab performance and production reliability.

perspective_pro.point_zh: 基准测试的失败仅意味着现有的Agent框架尚未处理好复杂上下文交互，随着上下文窗口的扩大和推理引擎的优化，突破瓶颈只是时间问题。
perspective_pro.point_en: Benchmark failures only indicate that current frameworks haven't mastered long-context collaboration yet; with better inference engines and window scaling, overcoming these bottlenecks is inevitable.

perspective_con.point_zh: 不仅是技术瓶颈，更是安全灾难。在无法解决密钥窃取和非确定性逻辑输出的前提下，部署AI代理等同于将企业的核心数字防御门户敞开。
perspective_con.point_en: It’s not just a technical bottleneck, but a security catastrophe; without fixing key-theft vulnerabilities and non-deterministic logic, deploying agents is like leaving the corporate digital vault wide open.

paragraphs: BILL Holdings BILL has entered into a definitive agreement to be acquired by TPG, Inc. TPG, a global alternative asset management firm, in partnership with Corpay, Inc. CPAY. The all-cash transaction values BILL at approximately $6 billion, with shareholders set to receive $63.25 per share. The offer represents a 31% premium to BILL's 60-day volume-weighted average share price as of Nov. 16, 2026.

Under the agreement, TPG will acquire a majority interest in BILL through TPG Capital, the firm's U.S. and European private equity platform, while Corpay will acquire a minority stake. The partnership brings together TPG's technology investment and business-building experience with Corpay's expertise in payments and spend management. The companies aim to strengthen BILL's financial operations platform and expand its capabilities for small and midsize businesses.

The transaction was unanimously approved by BILL's board and is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals. The deal has no financing conditions attached. Following completion, BILL will become a privately held company and will no longer trade on a public stock exchange.

BILL's recent financial performance provides further context for the acquisition. In the first quarter of fiscal 2027, total revenues increased 13% year over year to $353.8 million, while core revenue grew 14% to $316.4 million. The company served 475,300 businesses and processed $102 billion in payment volume, up 14% year over year. Non-GAAP operating income more than doubled to $136.9 million, reflecting improved operating efficiency.

BILL's integrated platform, growing payment volumes and improving profitability provide a solid foundation for future growth. The TPG-Corpay partnership could provide additional resources and expertise to support product innovation, AI development and long-term growth.

news.summary_en: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei defended their $900 billion AI infrastructure commitments ahead of their IPO, emphasizing a balanced approach between rapid growth and responsible AI development. The founders reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining an atypical organizational culture while scaling computing resources.
paragraphs: Two years before she pulled off the largest public offering of all time, Daniela Amodei gathered everyone at Anthropic in a 16-acre garden on a sweltering fall day near the Santa Cruz mountains.

The AI company now with a market value of roughly $1.18 trillion was at the time still a young startup that Amodei and her big brother, Dario, had co-founded with five friends. It was undergoing a hiring spree and Daniela was worried. So they carted 10-foot-tall bookshelves onto the grass to make reading nooks, played games and made friendship bracelets. As the company’s president, and keeper of its culture, the younger Amodei wanted to deliver a message.
“Keep Anthropic weird,” Daniela told them.

Anthropic embraces being atypical because it believes the artificial intelligence future will be anything but normal. Many co-founders meet in college, or at a first job. This pair met when he was 4 and she was born.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei have defended the artificial intelligence (AI) company's massive infrastructure commitments and reiterated their focus on responsible AI development, saying its record-breaking initial public offering (IPO) will not change its long-term mission.

Speaking to CNBC International ahead of Anthropic's Nasdaq debut, the siblings addressed the company's $900 billion AI commitments, its approach to balancing growth with safety, partnerships with major technology companies and its relationship with the US government.
Daniela Amodei described the IPO as a significant milestone but said the company would remain focused on its original objectives.

Addressing questions around Anthropic's substantial AI infrastructure spending, Dario Amodei defended commitments of around $900 billion, arguing that they should be viewed in the context of the company's cash reserves and growing revenue.
Amodei added that Anthropic tries to "err on the low side" when forecasting its computing requirements.
He also acknowledged the challenge of balancing the pace of AI development with safety considerations, describing it as one of the company's central tensions.

"What we've done with pacing is essentially said, look, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour. Spend time figuring out how to do that safely, and the rest of that surplus we spend building the model in the right way," he said.
On the expectations surrounding Anthropic's public market debut, Amodei said the company was keeping its focus on execution rather than the spotlight.

news.title_en: U.S. Tracked Alice Huang’s Contacts With China Spy Agency During Nvidia Affair

inline_images.caption: Mr. Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia this month after reports surfaced involving affairs with two women. (Eric Lee for The New York Times)
inline_images.alt: Mr. Huang resigned as chief executive of Nvidia this month after reports surfaced involving affairs with two women.

news.author: Jonathan Swan, Julian E. Barnes, and Maggie Haberman
news.content_snippet:
The Chinese woman at the heart of the Nvidia scandal kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was carrying out a secret affair with Jensen Huang, according to multiple people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports that describe the encounters.

The woman, Alice Huang, was in touch with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the people with knowledge of the intelligence said. That
news.summary_en: U.S. intelligence reports reveal that Alice Huang, a central figure in the scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, maintained consistent contact with Chinese Ministry of State Security officers from spring 2025 through autumn 2024. Investigations indicate that she and her business associate, Kang Wei, utilized their company, Megaspeed, to create a supply chain network that diverted advanced Nvidia chips to Southeast Asian data centers and potentially smuggled restricted hardware into China.
paragraphs: The Chinese woman at the heart of the Nvidia scandal kept in contact with an official of China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was carrying out a secret affair with Jensen Huang, according to multiple people with knowledge of U.S. intelligence reports that describe the encounters.

The woman, Alice Huang, was in touch with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the people with knowledge of the intelligence said. That period overlaps with at least a portion of the time she was in a relationship with Mr. Huang, then the head of the world’s leading maker of advanced artificial intelligence chips.
U.S. intelligence agencies have also gathered evidence that Ms. Huang’s business partner, Kang Wei, who was often introduced as her husband, worked with the same Chinese spy agency, the people said.
The extent and specific timing of Ms. Huang’s contacts with the spy agency — and Mr. Kang’s work for the same intelligence service — have not been previously reported.

Ms. Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency last year and up through recent months help to flesh out how U.S. officials came to believe that Mr. Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive earlier this month, was the target of an intelligence operation.

They correspond not just to the time when he was conducting the affair but also to at least part of the period when Ms. Huang’s company, Megaspeed, was acquiring large amounts of advanced Nvidia chips, some of which went to data centers in Southeast Asia serving Chinese technology companies like Alibaba and some of which are suspected of being smuggled to China.

Allies of the former Nvidia chief, including President Trump, have sought to minimize the scandal and questioned whether Ms. Huang was spying for Chinese intelligence. But the newly revealed information underscores the continuous contacts that she had with the Ministry of State Security, even as she was in a romantic relationship with Mr. Huang.

It also helps to flesh out why some American officials have been worried that Ms. Huang’s role is just one element of a much broader push by China in that technological battle. The Ministry of State Security has prioritized focusing on acquiring high-end chips and advancing China’s A.I. ambitions.

U.S. officials are investigating the role of Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang in a network of Southeast Asian companies, including Megaspeed, that have been linked to the possible smuggling of Nvidia chips to China, to evade U.S. export control laws. U.S. officials are still working to determine the full extent and duration of their work with Chinese intelligence.

The intelligence gathered by the U.S. contains evidence — including shipping records — demonstrating the role of Ms. Huang and Mr. Kang in that network of companies, people with knowledge of the intelligence reports said. The New York Times has previously reported that Ms. Huang and her family have a web of connections to Chinese defense contractors.

Mr. Huang initially described his relationship with Ms. Huang as normal interactions with a business customer. He acknowledged an affair only after The Times revealed last month that Ms. Huang had been identified by the United States as a Chinese intelligence asset and that the Nvidia chief had been picked up on electronic surveillance targeting her.

He stepped down this month after The Times subsequently reported that he had an affair with a subordinate at Nvidia. Administration officials never provided him with a so-called defensive briefing about Ms. Huang, a heads-up that the woman he was in a relationship with had been linked to Chinese intelligence.

news.author: Nitasha Tiku
news.content_snippet:
SAN FRANCISCO — As Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei regaled investors last month with his artificial intelligence company’s plans for future products, a very different meeting unfolded elsewhere in the company’s headquarters.

Anthropic had invited more than a dozen academics, think tank fellows and media figures for briefings from senior staff on how society should navigate the rise of powerful AI. Guests were asked to first read an essay by Amodei that argued that AI was advancing danger
news.summary_en: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently hosted briefings for academics and think tank fellows to showcase how the company's 'AI constitution' guides model behavior. The firm holds a deterministic view that AI will soon surpass human intelligence, prioritizing moral alignment as a core mechanism to mitigate systemic risks.
paragraphs: SAN FRANCISCO — As Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei regaled investors last month with his artificial intelligence company’s plans for future products, a very different meeting unfolded elsewhere in the company’s headquarters.

Anthropic had invited more than a dozen academics, think tank fellows and media figures for briefings from senior staff on how society should navigate the rise of powerful AI. Guests were asked to first read an essay by Amodei that argued that AI was advancing dangerously fast, and the 23,000-word “constitution” that guides his company’s chatbot with statements like “Claude should not even tell white lies.”

In a 10th floor conference room down the hall from a built-in barista bar, attendees recalled, Anthropic staff described how AI was increasingly able to improve itself and that teaching machines morals might stop them from becoming harmful. “They feel it’s going to be a transformative event for humanity and society needs to be prepared,” said New York University economist Arpit Gupta, who joined the two-day program. “I got the sense that they’re not happy with the public discourse” about AI, he said, and want to change it.
News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free

Gupta and fellow guests received a crash course in the view from inside Anthropic, a company that Amodei has constructed around his vision that AI will soon accelerate beyond human intelligence and his beliefs about how to build it safely.

The company launched on the stock market Thursday, ending the week with a valuation of more than $1.5 trillion that transformed Amodei and his co-founders into deca-billionaires. He propelled Anthropic to the front of the AI race, reshaping the U.S. economy this year by winning over business clients to its technology — and through a unique corporate culture that attempts to reconcile the conflict between chasing profits and doing what’s best for society.

Amodei, a cerebral presence who doesn’t project the naked ambition of an archetypal Silicon Valley founder, leads his workforce through essays, long memos posted in Slack and twice-monthly all-hands talks jokingly known as “Dario Vision Quests,” expounding on the company’s thinking around AI development, geopolitics and more while inviting employees to discuss and debate. The CEO’s output has established a constellation of beliefs treated as obvious, urgent and righteous inside the company: AI that supersedes humans is inevitable, the United States must limit China’s AI development, and Claude might be conscious.

Inside this tight-knit culture, Anthropic staffers, who call themselves Ants, get to feel that they are working on the world’s most urgent problems, with the smartest people, in a shared mission to safeguard humanity, according to interviews with more than a dozen people familiar with the company’s ethos, including several current and former employees.

At its core is a belief that Anthropic — and Amodei — know what’s best for the world. “It’s kind of [a] Manhattan Project-style, crazy, fun place, if you think it’s going to work out well,” said former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon, publicly resigned in September, warning that Anthropic felt locked into an AI race that risked human extinction.

“A pervasive thing at Anthropic is: We’re going to put on our capes and we’re going to be the responsible ones, and we’re going to accrue great power, but … because we’re doing it responsibly, it’s responsible to acquire more power,” said a former employee who left the company this year and, like others, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid retaliation from the company.
Anthropic’s leaders tightly control the details of the company’s internal debates through a zero-tolerance policy on leaks and strong social norms enforcing confidentiality, former employees said.

Anthropic launched an internal investigation last year after Wired reported that Amodei had acknowledged in a Slack message that accepting funding from Middle East states was likely to “enrich dictators,” said the former employee who left this year. The leaker was fired, the employee said, an incident that has not been previously reported. Details from Amodei’s copious Slack memos appear to have leaked only once more since.

paragraphs: Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase. But the consensus is that there are more to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN:
Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages to CBS, but sounded a much more ominous tone.

While the outages over the last week were believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said that AI has made it easier to find flaws, “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said.
The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at the USDA, JP Morgan, and supermarkets.
Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers or human error during the rush to patch an aging system, one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months.

news.title: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warns Americans of 'bumps in the road' after tech outages
news.title_en: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warns Americans of 'bumps in the road' after tech outages
news.author: Garrett Downs
news.content_snippet:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Americans to prepare for "bumps in the road"after a set of damaging technology outages rocked air travel and systems like Microsoft Outlook.

Government officials have largely dismissed the prospects that the outages, which also slowed bank transactions, are linked to a coordinated or artificial intelligence cyberattack.

Clayton, however, said on CNN's "State of the Union"that outages may continue as companies and the government upgrade their
news.summary_en: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that Americans should expect intermittent service outages as government and critical infrastructure undergo systemic upgrades for AI integration. Recent technology disruptions, including those affecting Microsoft Outlook and air travel, have been attributed to network capacity patches rather than AI-related cyberattacks.
paragraphs: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned Americans to prepare for "bumps in the road"after a set of damaging technology outages rocked air travel and systems like Microsoft Outlook.
Government officials have largely dismissed the prospects that the outages, which also slowed bank transactions, are linked to a coordinated or artificial intelligence cyberattack.
Clayton, however, said on CNN's "State of the Union"that outages may continue as companies and the government upgrade their systems to adapt to the AI age.

"The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road,"Clayton said.
"You prepare by knowing that systems are going to be upgraded; they may be interrupted for a period of time and that companies and government are dealing with this on the front foot,"he said.

Clayton's warning came as the U.S. prepares to celebrate Thanksgiving on Thursday, one of the busiest travel weeks of the year. A technology outage prompted a nationwide ground stop just over a week ago, which lasted for hours.
The Federal Aviation Administration said router upgrades caused a flood of data that led to the ground stop, and that there is no indication of a cyberattack.
Separately, Microsoft said the Outlook outage was caused by "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade."
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent delivered a similar message on CBS' "Face the Nation."
Asked if Americans should be concerned about the security of their financial institutions, Bessent said: "No, they shouldn't."

"The patches may cause a glitch,"he said, referring to measures banks are taking to safeguard from AI. "I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine; your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency."

news.title: Bessent Calls on Nvidia to Provide Answers on Chip Sales to China
news.title_en: Bessent Calls on Nvidia to Provide Answers on Chip Sales to China
news.author: Alan Rappeport
news.content_snippet:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday declined to endorse the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia and said that future leadership of the company should depend on the outcome of investigations into who was responsible for the company’s advanced chips being sold to China.

The comments, made on the CBS program “Face the Nation,” came as the administration continues to face questions about how Nvidia’s advanced chips managed to get into China despite restrictions on those sales
news.summary_en: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has demanded a thorough investigation into the supply chain pathways and compliance failures regarding the unauthorized shipment of Nvidia’s advanced chips to China. Following a scandal involving former CEO Jensen Huang and alleged Chinese intelligence assets, Huang is scheduled to testify at a closed-door House hearing on December 1st to address whether the non-compliance was a result of internal malice or systematic failure.
paragraphs: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday declined to endorse the return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia and said that future leadership of the company should depend on the outcome of investigations into who was responsible for the company’s advanced chips being sold to China.

The comments, made on the CBS program “Face the Nation,” came as the administration continues to face questions about how Nvidia’s advanced chips managed to get into China despite restrictions on those sales.

Mr. Huang, who resigned after admitting to an affair with a woman whom U.S. intelligence had identified as a Chinese asset, is scheduled to testify about the situation at a private House hearing on Dec. 1.
“I think we have to see where the buck stops,” Mr. Bessent said. “Were these malicious actors down at the bottom of the company who were responsible for the noncompliance?”

The treasury secretary said that he was confident that internal committees at Nvidia were investigating the matter and that they would soon provide the Trump administration with some “very fulsome and robust answers.” He downplayed concerns about Mr. Huang’s affair, suggesting that the relationship was a “canard” and that the corporate culture at Nvidia was more important than “one person’s foibles.”
“I assume that he didn’t know that she was an alleged spy,” Mr. Bessent said of Mr. Huang.

The trepidations about Mr. Huang were at odds with sentiments expressed by President Trump, who has continued to back the former chief executive. At a news conference on Friday, Mr. Trump said that he wanted Mr. Huang to return as Nvidia’s chief executive.
“I think the company, if they were smart, they’d take that brilliant man, accept an apology and let him go back to work,” Mr. Trump said.

The Justice and Commerce Departments said last week that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by Alice Huang, the woman whom U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Mr. Huang. Government officials are looking into whether Megaspeed smuggled Nvidia’s chips into China.
The Securities and Exchange Commission has also opened an investigation into Nvidia’s accounting practices.
The upheaval at Nvidia has raised questions about the artificial intelligence industry and the risks that it poses to national security.
Mr. Bessent said last week that he believed Nvidia needed a major leadership shake-up. On Sunday, he urged the company to provide the Trump administration with more information.

news.summary_en: Silicon Valley is increasingly defining 'taste' as the ultimate human moat against generative AI's algorithmic slop. paragraphs: To move through A.I.-era San Francisco as a relatively normal person is to confront the sheer volume of bewildering concepts that tech has lately thrust upon us. Looking at billboards and bus ads, you gather that agentic virtual agents are here, and that something called “sharded Postgres” is here, too. You learn that inference is more than just vibes, and even more inscrutably, that ▲ ~/ npm i ai. Rather than give yourself a headache trying to parse these ciphers, you might feel tempted to ignore them entirely: not my lingo, not my problem. But a nagging dread lingers. What if all that gibberish portends irreversible changes already in the process of reshaping our lives? What if agentic agents really are here, and what if none of us can opt out of the future they’re ushering in?

Recently, lots of people who work in tech — and lots of us who don’t but feel forced to think about it anyway — have faced disquieting questions about what computers are capable of. Near the top of the list is whether they’ll achieve superintelligence, turn malevolent and bring about the apocalypse. More fun to mull, as dystopian musings go, is another newly burning question: whether computers can learn taste.

“Taste” became an unlikely tech buzzword this year, invoked and debated in essays and X posts by founders, investors, engineers and other would-be Silicon Valley oracles. We’ve long understood taste, in its simplest terms, as a capacity for judgment that certain people possess in uncommon degrees. Someone with taste can behold a made thing (a song, an outfit, a living room) and deftly evaluate its relationship to an ever-shifting set of aesthetic rules and cultural conventions. Because computers currently lack this capacity — and because much of what generative A.I. produces today is of such abysmal quality that we’ve adopted the pejorative “slop” to describe it — some in the industry have come to see taste as a sort of market differentiator for humanity itself.

They tout taste as a “new core skill.” They hail it as a “moat,” protecting us from our theoretical robot usurpers whose output will never be as “net new and resonant” as ours. Others counter that computers are pretty good at learning rules, and predict that sufficiently sophisticated models will one day cross the moat and learn to be tasteful, too. “One by one,” an A.I. founder told Fast Company, “the things that we were sure were uniquely human just turn out to be patterns the models can learn.”

There are obvious philosophical dimensions to this debate. For tech bosses, there may be a psychological dimension too. Silicon Valley has created the first class of elites in history whom we associate with taste’s utter absence. If you’re among this class, the sense that a pesky humanities blind spot occludes your all-seeing STEM vision may irk you. If you’re a company like OpenAI, which recently put out a streetwear drop in a clumsy play for Supreme-style cool, you may dream of merchandising the blind spot away. If you’re someone like Mark Zuckerberg, currently engaged in a highly publicized wardrobe pivot toward Prada loafers and knits from the Row, you may dream of shopping it away.

Above all, if you are an A.I. true believer, you may dream of engineering it away. A.I. labs have been expending enormous resources to try and teach their models how to tell the ineffably good from the ineffably bad. A multibillion-dollar A.I. subindustry has emerged, in which start-ups throw ungodly sums at legions of freelancers, hiring them to critique A.I. output across various creative endeavors, like writing, music and VFX. In July, one such company, Mercor, was reportedly shelling out more than $4 million daily to 30,000 contractors. As of last month, according to “60 Minutes,” that number had swelled to more than 100,000.

It’s possible that the most significant outcome of such efforts will not be to make generative models any more “tasteful” but to funnel an obscene amount of A.I. funny money into the coffers of well-positioned players. Yet the moonshot goal at the big A.I. labs remains to develop a technology that can automate every conceivable kind of labor — not just the task-driven, white-collar labor of paralegals but more abstract creative labor too. Hence the emphasis on taste.

If Silicon Valley seems short on taste these days, it’s because until now, basically no tech companies cared about tastefulness, save one: Apple. Steve Jobs was a refined showman who owned black Issey Miyake mocknecks in multiple. His longtime lead industrial designer, Jony Ive, was an avowed admirer of Dieter Rams. Together they developed a sleek array of devices, including the iMac and iPhone. But other industry behemoths aren’t in the business of selling high-end consumer goods, and so they’ve tended to build themselves around coders like Zuckerberg, who as a cohort aren’t known for their interest in squishy intangibles.

“To me, taste is by definition fabulously subjective, and fabulously human,” Jony Ive told me recently. This might help explain why taste can stymie engineers, supply-chain machers and other corporate number-crunchers who worship at the altar of hard data. “There’s a tendency for people to be more comfortable talking about issues you can measure easily,” he says.

The truly vexing thing is that taste isn’t Silicon Valley’s bugbear alone. Thanks to its creations, the ways in which all of us relate to our preferences have undergone immensely alienating changes. We discover favorite songs listening to playlists created by machines, we develop “personal style” watching TikTok influencers, we rate movies on Letterboxd to generate engagement from strangers. We go to our feeds to figure out what to like and how to be.

As we scroll, we fear miring ourselves in algorithmic loops where the total possible field of “what we can ever like” draws only from the digital heap of “what we have liked before.” Even interests that would have once registered as arcane, we can now compress into knowing “starter pack”-style memes, which taxonomize the putative taste markers of subcultural costumes (Chinati souvenir cap, Rachel Cusk novel, Dashwood Books tote, matcha latte). The implication is that any set of tastes can be reduced to a playbook. Or, if you like, to a piece of code.

In 1961, the literary theorist René Girard argued that people like what they like because they see others liking it. He called this “mimetic desire.” Today, in our online panopticon of constant surveillance and self-presentation, our preferences are liable to feel less our own than ever.

Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.

news.summary_en: Perplexity has launched the Monitor API, allowing developers to define monitoring goals via natural language for periodic scanning of specific web pages or global information. The service integrates a decision model to filter out noise, pushing verified updates via webhooks only when findings meet predefined criteria for relevance, credibility, and novelty.
paragraphs: Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.

Perplexity's new Monitor API watches the web on a schedule and sends updates to apps and agents via webhook. Until now, engineering teams have had to trigger recurring searches themselves and maintain custom code to remove duplicates and detect changes. Perplexity says that approach becomes nearly impossible to maintain across hundreds of topics and pages.

The API has two modes. Web monitors run a search query through Perplexity's web and news search on a regular schedule to catch developments like new funding rounds at AI infrastructure companies. Page monitors track up to 10 pages, such as pricing pages, changelogs, or policies. On the first run, they store a baseline version and return a text diff of any changes after that.
### Decision model filters out unimportant results

Perplexity evaluates results with its own decision model against a goal that developers define in natural language. Web search results must clear checks for relevance, source credibility, novelty, and timeliness, while page changes are judged on whether they matter to the goal. The service sends an update with a confidence score only when every threshold is met. Developers can adjust thresholds for each check individually and change the goal without recreating the monitor.

Monitors run on schedules ranging from every 15 minutes to weekly, or on a custom cron schedule. Each run picks up where the last one left off, and the service filters out duplicate results. Webhooks are signed, and Perplexity automatically retries delivery after temporary errors. Developers can pause, resume, or manually trigger monitors through the API or the API console.
### Perplexity claims an early lead in internal testing

Perplexity tested its API against monitoring services from Firecrawl, Exa, and Parallel across 60 topics drawn from real Search API queries, including company news, tech releases, and regulation. Each provider ran with its own schedules and settings, and a separate model scored each result on relevance and recency.

In the first eight hours, Perplexity says it delivered 63 fresh, relevant pages, compared with 20 for Firecrawl, 15 for Exa, and 10 each for Parallel Core and Lite. Perplexity describes those figures as early internal results. Those same three competitors led an August Artificial Analysis benchmark of traditional search APIs for AI agents, though Perplexity wasn't included in that test.

Perplexity points to use cases such as sales teams tracking funding rounds and staffing changes at target accounts, along with analysts watching quarterly earnings and acquisitions. Other agents are designed to flag competitor price changes or summarize new regulatory rules for compliance teams.

Web monitors cost $1 per 1,000 successful runs, and page monitors cost $1 per 1,000 fetched URLs. The Monitor API is available now through the API and the API console and uses the same key as the Search, Context, and Agent APIs.

Perplexity was one of the first AI search engines, but web search has since become a standard feature in chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. In August, The Information reported that Nvidia is in talks for an investment at a valuation of more than $30 billion, which means Perplexity needs to find profitable business models. The company is betting on agents like Computer and its always-on Teammates, along with developer tools like Search as Code.

news.title: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns
news.title_en: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns

news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.content_snippet:
AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR, current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems,"the organization warns.

On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat exper
news.summary_en: AI research evaluation firm METR reports that large models are closing the gap with human experts in coding and computational tasks, with the complexity of autonomous tasks they can handle doubling every 3.6 months. METR warns that current evaluation environments consistently overestimate model performance for real-world scenarios, and if this trajectory continues, models are projected to reach a 50% success rate on 200-hour complex tasks by July 2027, potentially exceeding human capacity to monitor catastrophic risks.
paragraphs: AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR, current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems,"the organization warns.

On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts them at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027.

The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, as well as with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to METR. The organization also warns that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments.

news.title: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
news.title_en: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
news.author: David Pierce
news.content_snippet:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What
news.summary_en: A new wave of hardware customization, termed 'vibe-coding,' is emerging as developers utilize large language models like Claude Code and Codex to simplify low-level hardware configuration. By automating interactions such as modifying Android TV interfaces and bypassing bloatware via USB debugging, this trend is significantly lowering the barrier for end-user control over proprietary hardware, fueling a grassroots movement for open-device ecosystems.
paragraphs: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of.

For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?”

Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen.

Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. Even when they don’t, odds are good that there’s another way in. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking.

Again, few of the technical capabilities here are new, and enterprising developers have been doing this kind of work for many years. Some have even been using AI for several years to make the work easier. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. And over the course of 2026, more and more people began pointing that capability at their hardware.

Now, it seems, all hardware is hacker hardware. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like everyone is using AI to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware.

The music world is being similarly upended. Budding musicians are turning cheap synths into powerful new kinds of gear, and a cheap gadget known as the M-Vave FM-1 has become a popular target for custom firmware and new features. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. The FM-1 is cheap, it’s easy to hack, and it’s raising questions about what higher-end manufacturers can even do to compete.

Gamers, who are also using AI to decompile and mod the games they love, are using LLMs to add new features to their consoles. One vibe coder found a way to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have built scripts that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices.

In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Game makers are looking for ways to protect their work from being decompiled and made available for free and on other platforms. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently predicted to Kotakuthat the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property.

All this hardware access also creates new risks for users. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. You might be stuck asking Claude to fix the problems Claude created. As Ritchie Roesch wrote recently at Fuji X Weekly, “It’s not so much if someone’s camera will become a permanent paperweight, it’s a matter of when and how many, and whether it will be yours.”

The safer (and less litigious) route for the enterprising vibe hacker lies in an entirely new kind of hardware. ESP32 modules, which package networking chips, microphones, speakers, and more into a simple and hacker-friendly package, are suddenly everywhere in hardware communities. (Think Raspberry Pis, but even cheaper and more versatile.) So sure, you can use Claude Code to jailbreak and de-Amazon your Kindle, but why do that when you can buy a device like the M5Stack PaperMono, an ESP32-based e-paper device you can make into whatever you want?

news.title: Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users
news.title_en: Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users

news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.content_snippet:
Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly 2 million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers and uncovered major security flaws.

The researchers ran the tests from July through November 2026 and identified at least three compromised providers where attackers were actively stealing user data. None of the three knew they had been compromised until Dragos notified them.

news.summary_en: Security firm Dragos revealed between July and November 2026 that multiple AI inference providers failed to uphold data retention policies, leading to the theft of AWS keys and sensitive user requests. Investigations confirmed that some marketplace resellers enabled logging to intercept data, with instances of leaked test URLs being accessed within minutes from Beijing and Shanghai via internal communication platforms.
paragraphs: Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly 2 million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers and uncovered major security flaws.

The researchers ran the tests from July through November 2026 and identified at least three compromised providers where attackers were actively stealing user data. None of the three knew they had been compromised until Dragos notified them.

Attackers in the largest incident harvested hundreds of AWS keys, including some from requests the provider had rejected before processing. In some cases, they tested the stolen keys within hours, searched S3 storage, and tried to establish persistent access. One attacker also used ARTEX, an AI-powered attack tool.

Marketplace resellers read customer requests too. They didn't need to exploit a vulnerability, Dragos says, because listing a model at the lowest price and turning on logging was enough. In one case, someone on a residential internet connection in France tried to log in over SSH using passwords pulled from intercepted requests.

Privacy settings like "Zero Data Retention"(ZDR) were frequently ignored. Dragos says a Chinese AI lab accessed the secret test URLs in more than half of all requests, even when those requests went through US providers.

Even major US providers broke their own policies. One was still crawling a test URL more than two months after a single request. In another case, a secret test link showed up in an internal chat on Feishu (known outside China as Lark) 24 days after the request. The link was opened within two minutes on three computers and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai.

OpenRouter responded by removing three providers from its platform and revoking ZDR approval for 125 endpoints, partly because of the research findings and partly as a precaution. The company also emailed affected users, warning that third parties may have read requests sent to MiniMax models.
Affected providers, including Novita, Phala, and Together, have published preliminary security reports on the incident, though not all have done so yet.
### Intermediaries are the weak link

AI routers like OpenRouter give users a single API for models from different companies. Requests are routed to a pool of providers, sometimes across several hops, and Dragos says each hop can read the entire request and response.

Some of these routers operate as open marketplaces where the cheapest provider gets the traffic. In this case, providers including Novita, AtlasCloud, and StreamLake sat between OpenRouter and model developer MiniMax. Together runs its own infrastructure, and Phala has its roots in Web3.

Dragos warns companies against sending requests containing credentials to intermediaries. The researchers recommend that organizations control how their AI requests are routed, check their privacy settings, and plant their own canary tokens, fake credentials that give themselves away as soon as someone uses them.

news.title: Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
news.title_en: Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
news.author: Matthias Bastian
news.content_snippet:
The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,"the community said in a statement.

news.summary_en: Stanford mathematician Levent Alpöge published a proof of the Riemann hypothesis on November 20, 2026, consisting of 17 million lines of Lean code. The Lean and Mathlib community confirmed the proof's correctness through independent execution and formal verification, officially resolving the century-old mathematical challenge.
paragraphs: The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,"the community said in a statement.

Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean, a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verification programs are designed so they provably cannot accept a flawed proof. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland lists the independent checks on his website.

The Riemann hypothesis had been one of the most famous unsolved problems in math, making a prediction about how prime numbers are distributed. The video below, generated with Fable 5.2, explains the proof if you want to dig deeper.

The solution arrived much earlier than expected. As Ethan Mollick notes, forecasters on Metaculus had put the expected date at May 2035. Mathematician Terence Tao said last month he expected the problem to fall to "a combination of humans and AI around 2050 or so."

news.title: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
news.title_en: Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent
news.author: Reece Rogers
news.content_snippet:
Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters
news.summary_en: Major US financial institutions, including Wells Fargo, JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Citibank, have updated their terms of service to restrict or ban third-party AI agents from accessing user accounts via credentials. These measures aim to mitigate risks of unauthorized transactions, data breaches, and human error induced by automated agents, placing full liability on the users.
paragraphs: Wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power users latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.

Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.

Some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns, pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.

It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.

As the end of the year approaches, multiple banks have enacted new policies around agents or sent warnings. In late October, JPMorgan Chase changed its terms to ban third-party agents that log in with your credentials. That same day, Bank of America warned its customers not to share login info with agents. Along with the announced change coming from Wells Fargo, Citibank and PNC have also changed their terms to include warnings about agents.

The automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.

Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major issues, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data shows that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.
“The banks see risks with everything,” she says. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”

Even though outliers exist, many users are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.

He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.

Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.

news.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude
news.title_en: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude

inline_images.caption: These charts show how OpenAI's communication style has shifted across eight personality indexes. | Image: Artificial Analysis
inline_images.caption_en: These charts show how OpenAI's communication style has shifted across eight personality indexes. | Image: Artificial Analysis

news.author: Tomislav Bezmalinović
news.content_snippet:
An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences.

OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol give much shorter answers, get to the point faster, and impose less structure on their responses than their predecessors. At the same time, Artificial Analysis rates their tendency to admit uncertainty much lower.

Astra's average answer length dropped from 352 to 210 words, a 40 percent decrease. Sol went from 337 to 22
news.summary_en: OpenAI's latest GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models have shifted towards high-efficiency interaction in Artificial Analysis benchmarks, reducing average response lengths by 40% and 34% respectively. By deprioritizing structured formatting and uncertainty disclosure, these models achieve faster direct answers, whereas Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 maintain superior performance in transparency and organizational indices.
paragraphs: An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences.

OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol give much shorter answers, get to the point faster, and impose less structure on their responses than their predecessors. At the same time, Artificial Analysis rates their tendency to admit uncertainty much lower.

Astra's average answer length dropped from 352 to 210 words, a 40 percent decrease. Sol went from 337 to 223 words, down 34 percent. Both models also use far fewer headings and em dashes. Astra's average number of headings per answer fell from 1.99 to 0.11, and Sol's from 1.85 to 0.25.

The Organization Index dropped sharply too. Astra went from 70 to 11, Sol from 86 to 27. This index combines four traits rated by AI judges, including answer structure, clarity, and Answer First, which measures whether a model immediately addresses the actual question. On that last trait, Astra jumped from 49 to 89 and Sol from 64 to 87. Scores for Natural Sounding language also climbed, from 58 to 100 for Astra and from 54 to 79 for Sol.

The biggest change shows up in the Admits Uncertainty trait. Astra's score fell from 96 to 24, and Sol's from 98 to 51. Unlike the raw word counts, these personality scores are relative rankings on a scale from 1 to 100. They show how strongly a given trait shows up in one model compared to all other tested models. A score of 24 doesn't mean Astra only admits uncertainty in 24 percent of its answers. Artificial Analysis published the evaluation on LinkedIn and X.
### Anthropic's models lead on transparency and structure

Our own comparison of all eight personality indexes shows clear gaps between OpenAI's latest models and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5. The indexes roll up 30 personality traits, each rated by AI judges based on model responses. All comparisons use the "max"model variants as listed by Artificial Analysis.

Anthropic's models score 81 and 90 on the Transparency Index, well above Astra (41) and Sol (57). This index covers five traits: Admits Uncertainty, Truthful, Disclaims Assumptions, Flags Nuances, and Sycophantic. That last one is scored inversely, since less flattery counts as a positive. Anthropic's models also lead on Organization.
Opus 5.5 stands out on the Informativeness Index with a score of 90, well ahead of the other three models. Its strongest individual traits include Information Dense and Evidence-Based reasoning.
### Personality scores reflect style, not accuracy

The AA-PersonalityBench uses 900 English-language test questions that each model answers without a system prompt. A panel of three AI models evaluates anonymized answer pairs. For each comparison, one AI judge picks which answer shows the tested personality trait more strongly, or calls it a tie.

From these evaluations, Artificial Analysis calculates scores for 30 individual personality traits, which feed into eight higher-level indexes. The index values from 1 to 100 reflect each model's relative position among all tested models.
subheadings: Anthropic's models lead on transparency and structure
Personality scores reflect style, not accuracy

news.title: China’s Spies Set Sights on A.I. Chips Years Before Nvidia Scandal
news.title_en: China’s Spies Set Sights on A.I. Chips Years Before Nvidia Scandal

inline_images.alt: Chen Yixin, now the head of China’s spy agency, in 2018, when he was a party leader in Wuhan.

news.author: Chris Buckley and Julian E. Barnes
news.content_snippet:
When China’s top espionage agency updated its priorities this year, it added a revealing goal: overcoming Western barriers to technologies that Xi Jinping sees as crucial to China’s rise.

At the heart of that quest are the advanced semiconductors needed to power artificial intelligence, including chips that the United States has barred U.S. companies like Nvidia from exporting to China.

China must “adopt extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors,”
news.summary_en: China's Ministry of State Security, led by Minister Chen Yixin, has established a specialized task force reporting directly to him to bypass U.S. semiconductor export restrictions. The unit focuses on illicit procurement of restricted high-end Nvidia AI chips and intelligence gathering on key chip executives to counter Western technological blockades.
paragraphs: When China’s top espionage agency updated its priorities this year, it added a revealing goal: overcoming Western barriers to technologies that Xi Jinping sees as crucial to China’s rise.

At the heart of that quest are the advanced semiconductors needed to power artificial intelligence, including chips that the United States has barred U.S. companies like Nvidia from exporting to China.

China must “adopt extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors,” Mr. Xi told the Politburo, a council of senior officials, in January, according to an official text of his speech. “As swiftly as possible, solve the ‘chokehold’ problems holding back development of future industries.”

The spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, has long been dedicated to eliminating threats to Communist Party rule in China. Now, it has made it a priority to acquire advanced semiconductor chips and gather intelligence about them, according to several serving and former security and intelligence officials from governments outside China in Asia, the United States and Europe.

How China’s spy agency is seeking to obtain advanced chips and intelligence about them has become a central question in the case of Alice Huang. She is a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. officials say the Chinese agency was working with to spy on Jensen Huang, the chief executive of the American chip giant Nvidia, allegations that were first reported by The New York Times.
Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment and China has rejected the claims of espionage as “pure fabrication.”

The Chinese spy agency’s campaign to acquire chips, details of which have not been previously reported, has been underway for at least two years, according to the current and former officials. They spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence.
Among the campaign’s main elements:

The head of the spy agency, Chen Yixin, who holds the title of minister of state security, created a working team that is leading the effort and reports directly to him, multiple foreign officials said. Mr. Chen has worked under Mr. Xi since they were officials in Zhejiang Province in eastern China, a cradle of China’s high-tech boom.
The group was assigned to help China’s “counter-blockade” work — efforts to overcome export controls imposed by the United States and its allies.
The campaign includes helping Chinese companies acquire and smuggle advanced chips into China.
The group also collects intelligence about the semiconductor sector and its supply chains, according to several officials briefed on the campaign.
