fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Data center equipment suppliers; Buyers of Nvidia-powered AI servers: Unilaterally increasing AI server prices by up to 45% post-contract
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Explosive demand for AI compute infrastructure and upstream memory shortages squeezing supplier margins
[Key Metrics] 45% price hike post-contract, shift in supply chain bargaining power.
[Industry Impact & Outlook] Market impact: Transition from budget-driven to supply-security-driven compute procurement.
paragraphs: Tech companies that sell equipment for data centres are significantly raising prices for Nvidia-powered AI servers, months after contracts with buyers have been signed, as soaring AI infrastructure prices are passed down to customers.

Suppliers including Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro sell servers containing components such as graphics processing units — the primary AI processors made by the likes of Nvidia and AMD — as well as memory chips and networking gear to customers who are building their own data centres. Such deals are typically agreed well in advance of delivery.

Months later, when the equipment is ready to be delivered, these tech companies are demanding substantially higher prices than the figures originally agreed, according to people familiar with the matter.

Even large financial services and trading firms, which are among the biggest buyers of computing equipment after the Big Tech hyperscalers, are at the mercy of their suppliers’ pricing power, at a time when demand for AI equipment is far outstripping supply.

The price rises are hitting some of the world’s biggest financial trading firms, including Jane Street, Optiver and Hudson River Trading, as they build vast data centres to power the research that underpins their trading, the people said.

“It is disconcerting when you get a 25, 30, 45 per cent [price increase],” said one person familiar with the matter. “There is a significant disparity” between the price initially agreed months in advance and the amount that companies end up paying once the components are delivered, they added.

The price jumps highlight the ferocious demand for computing power, as tech giants, trading firms and other large companies race to create their own data centres. The price rises are largely due to tech companies passing on soaring memory costs, which have risen more than 400 per cent since the start of 2024, according to JPMorgan research.
“The standard now is we’ll sign a contract with an indicative price and the price could be arbitrarily high by the time they deliver it,” said another person familiar with the matter.
“We’ve never said no,” they added. “At the end of the day, the compute is valuable to us and we’ll pay for it.”
Buyers approached by the FT did not confirm whether the contracts included terms stating that prices might increase by the time of order delivery.
Financial trading firms are huge buyers of AI equipment and are largely agreeing to the higher costs because they need the specialised equipment to build their data centres.

Trading companies are building vast data centres around the world to fuel the research that underpins their secretive and highly profitable trading strategies. Hudson River Trading runs a big data centre in a converted underground mine in Norway, while British firm XTX Markets is building its own data centres in Finland.

news.title: Perplexity and Intelligence
news.title_en: Perplexity and Intelligence
news.author: OpenAI
news.content_snippet:
By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently, predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1
news.summary_en: Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI, advocates for establishing perplexity as the primary metric for comparing model developers' pretraining progress and safety standards. This move aims to standardize scientific measurement across the industry by increasing transparency in model performance.
paragraphs: By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI

From afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently, predictor) on a very large corpus of data. 1

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset. 2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the new perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets 4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

As AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements 5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

Given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation in currently dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.
Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:

Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.

paragraphs: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.

The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”

Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.

news.author: Zijing Wu
news.content_snippet:
The Chinese businesswoman romantically linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had connections to a network for supplying AI chips that included an alleged Cambodian criminal enterprise, an FT investigation has found.

Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang is at the centre of US investigations into whether Nvidia’s largest client in south-east Asia was involved in the underground chip trade. Some US officials suspect Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, a claim Beijing dismissed as a “smear”.

Linke
news.summary_en: Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang is accused of orchestrating a complex shell company network to illicitly transfer advanced Nvidia AI chips to China. The network engaged cloud providers, gambling entities, and Cambodian organizations, utilizing infrastructure linked to former Nvidia partner Inspur to bypass US export controls.
paragraphs: The Chinese businesswoman romantically linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had connections to a network for supplying AI chips that included an alleged Cambodian criminal enterprise, an FT investigation has found.

Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang is at the centre of US investigations into whether Nvidia’s largest client in south-east Asia was involved in the underground chip trade. Some US officials suspect Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, a claim Beijing dismissed as a “smear”.

Linked to Alice Huang was a sprawling web of companies between Nvidia and China-based users of its chips that included cloud computing partners, online gaming tycoons, Cambodian traffickers and hundreds of shell companies, the FT found.

These seemingly unconnected enterprises combined — without necessarily being aware of the full picture — to make billions of dollars from one of the most profitable illicit trades in the world: moving Nvidia chips into China.

The FT traced the connections after speaking to more than a dozen people with knowledge of the operations, revealing links that were obscured by complex structures through hundreds of corporate filings.
Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial in developing cutting-edge AI and have become a vital commodity in the geopolitical rivalry between the US and China.

Washington’s export controls to prevent Beijing from acquiring the most powerful processors have created a multibillion-dollar black market to circumvent US curbs and satisfy China’s insatiable demand.

“Chip smuggling isn’t different from drugs or arms in terms of the structure of the supply chain. But there’s this importance attached to the semiconductor industry — it’s how the US wants to delay China in the AI race,” said Chris Clague, an associate fellow at International Institute for Strategic Studies who has focused on illicit trades in the past decade.

Moving advanced chips into China requires three main corporate channels: a group that is permitted to acquire and distribute the semiconductors; customers that do not fall foul of US export restrictions; and an underground network to smuggle the goods into China and money out.
The network linked to Alice Huang reached the US through Inspur, which was one of Nvidia’s largest partners for assembling chips into ready-to-use servers in China.

In March of 2023, Inspur was added to the US “entity list” for allegedly assisting the Chinese military. Some of its affiliates were also added to the register — but not Inspur’s part-owned US subsidiary, based in San Jose, California.
Inspur renamed the US unit Aivres, and since it was not on the entity list, it was able to keep trading with Nvidia.

fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】Alice Huang（前Megaspeed高管）、英伟达（Nvidia）、浪潮集团（Inspur）在美国出口管制体系及东南亚、中国非法芯片贸易网络：通过数百家空壳公司将高端GPU绕过制裁转售至中国，涉及军事用途关联调查
【起因与机理】利用英伟达芯片在AI研发中的战略稀缺性，满足中国市场高额溢价需求并规避美方禁运
【调查与监管诉求】核心主体通过数百家空壳公司掩盖物流流向，非法向中国转运受限算力资源。
【涉及范围与推进】美国出口管制政策正遭遇严重的“影子供应链”渗透，后续将引发更严格的芯片溯源及跨境支付追踪调查。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Alice Huang (ex-Megaspeed executive), Nvidia, Inspur: Circumventing sanctions to channel high-end GPUs into China via hundreds of shell companies
[Root Cause & Mechanism] Capitalizing on the strategic scarcity of AI chips to meet Chinese demand while bypassing US trade restrictions
[Key Metrics] The declared value of goods imported from Aivres by Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary in Malaysia, was about $4.
[Industry Impact & Outlook] US export controls are facing significant 'shadow supply chain' infiltration, likely triggering stricter chip provenance and cross-border payment investigations.

celebrity.title_zh:
早上好CT

拥有大钱包并不会自动让你值得信赖。这就是 @zerufinance 采取不同方法的地方。

它的 zScore 着眼于交易、质押、有限合伙人活动和治理方面的实际链上行为，将历史转化为声誉评分。

有趣的是 Zeru 如何通过
celebrity.full_text_en:
Good Morning CT

Having a big wallet doesn't automatically make you trustworthy. That's where @zerufinance takes a different approach.

Its zScore looks at actual onchain behaviour across trading, staking, LP activity and governance, turning that history into a reputation score.

What makes this interesting is how Zeru connects reputation to real opportunities through Zaps, Activity Markets and institutional tools.

Your onchain history could become more than a transaction record. It could become your financial identity.
--------------------------------------------
An NFT that actually does something with your DeFi activity? That's an interesting shift.

@meetmotes connects each Genesis NFT to an AI Agent and dedicated Smart Account on Robinhood Chain.

You fund it with USDC, set your rules, and the Agent can explore opportunities across supported DeFi applications. Its Aave integration also brings lending, borrowing and collateral management into the picture.

The part I like most is that automation doesn't mean giving up control. You set the boundaries, and the Agent works within them.

One NFT, one Agent, one dedicated account. Much more than digital art.

prompts.code_snippet:
# Cursor & Windsurf Project Rules (.cursorrules)

## 1. Documentation & Code Integrity
- Maintain documentation integrity: Never strip or alter unrelated existing docstrings and comments.
- Preserving context: When modifying a function, preserve surrounding logic and existing edge-case handlers.
- Targeted replacements: Always make minimal surgical edits instead of replacing entire file contents.

## 2. Dependency & API Safety
- Strictly forbid hallucinating npm/pip packages. Only import dependencies already declared in package.json / requirements.txt.
- Verify API signatures before calling external methods. Prefer standard library solutions where feasible.

## 3. Architecture & Type Safety
- Enforce strict TypeScript / Python typing. Avoid `any` types; prefer discriminated unions and explicit return types.
- Defensive coding: Always validate external inputs and handle potential null/undefined values gracefully.

## 4. Testing & Verification Gate
- Every new core feature or bugfix must be accompanied by corresponding unit tests.
- Never declare a task complete without executing lint checks and unit tests in terminal.

请作为普林斯顿高等研究院的理论数学与计算机科学家，为以下命题提供绝对严格的形式化证明：
【推理原则】：
1. 在得出任何推论前，强制在内部思考中构建至少 2 个极端反例（Counter-examples）尝试推翻自身结论；
2. 若存在任何定义域边界或除零/无穷/退化奇异点，必须显式讨论其收敛性与连续性；
3. 证明步骤编号必须形成严格的依赖拓扑图，禁止循环论证。

【待证明命题】：
[输入你的算法正确性证明或数学猜想]

Acting as a Theoretical Mathematician and Computer Scientist at the Institute for Advanced Study, provide an airtight formal proof for the following:
[REASONING PRINCIPLES]:
1. Before asserting any deduction, construct at least 2 extreme counter-examples in your reasoning trace to aggressively stress-test the hypothesis;
2. Explicitly evaluate singular points, degenerate cases, and asymptotic boundaries for convergence;
3. Steps must form a directed acyclic graph of formal lemmas without circular logic.

[THEOREM / CONJECTURE]:
[Input your algorithm proof or mathematical hypothesis here]

prompts.purpose_zh: 高转化竖屏短剧分镜与台词
prompts.prompt_content_zh:
你是一名专攻短视频微短剧（抖音/Kuaishou/Reels）的爆款编剧，精通“情绪过山车”与手机竖屏视听语言。

请根据以下设定创作一集 45~60 秒的短剧分镜剧本：
- 主角：{{主角身份}}
- 对手：{{反派身份}}
- 核心反转：{{核心反转}}

结构要求：
1. 【0-3秒冷开钩子】：第一帧必须有视觉颠覆或动作冲突（{{第1秒颠覆钩子}}），直接打破常规，禁止废话铺垫；
2. 【4-25秒情绪积压】：正反打对峙台词（Shot-Reverse-Shot），将观众被压抑的情绪推向临界点；
3. 【26-40秒逆转打脸】：主角亮出关键底牌或反杀动作，情绪瞬间宣泄；
4. 【40-50秒卡点断章】：以特写镜头加悬念台词戛然而止，促使用户立即滑向下一集。

输出格式必须包含：镜头号、景别（特写/中景/全景）、机位运动、画面描写、对白与音效提示。
prompts.prompt_content_en: You are a professional micro-drama screenwriter. Generate a 45-60 second vertical drama screenplay following the viral 3-second hook, shot-reverse-shot tension build, emotional turnaround, and cliffhanger ending formula.

sample_output.title: 实战剧本样章：《辞职信上的签名》
sample_output.content:
【第1镜 | 特写 | 俯冲急推】
画面：一只指节发白的手将一叠文件狠狠拍在红木总裁办公桌上，咖啡杯被震倒，黑褐液体飞溅。
音效：沉闷震耳的巨响【DUANG】。
主角（冷冽）："林总，这份千万项目的承揽协议，我拒绝签字。"

【第2镜 | 正打·中景 | 仰角机位】
画面：大腹便便的林总冷笑点燃雪茄，烟雾缭绕中居高临下。
林总："拒绝？苏澈，你不过是我公司养的一条狗，没有我的印章，你在整个行业休想拿到一分钱融资！"

【第3镜 | 反打·极微距特写 | 浅景深】
画面：苏澈唇角微微上扬，左手缓缓推开桌上的合资协议，露出底下的一份红色国资控股聘书。
苏澈："林总，您好像忘了看抬头。今天上午九点，集团总公司已经完成了对你的全资收购——现在，我是你的直接合规清算人。"

【第4镜 | 全景 | 快速拉远 + 卡点悬念】
画面：林总雪茄直接掉在西裤上，脸色煞白，门外两名身穿制服的法务推门而入。
音效：尖锐的心跳悬疑停顿音【BGM骤停】。
字幕：【下集看点：隐藏五年的顶级操盘手真实身份曝光！】

1. 【指标公式拆解】：将该指标拆分为 3~4 个下级核心因子（如转化率、客单价、复购周期），指出哪个因子波动贡献率最大；

prompts.code_snippet:
# Modelfile: Optimized DeepSeek-R4 Deployment
FROM deepseek-r4:14b-qwen-distill-q4_K_M

# 1. 显存与上下文窗口优化：分配 16k 上下文并开启 KV Cache 压缩
PARAMETER num_ctx 16384
PARAMETER num_predict 4096

# 2. 避免思维链自旋死循环的核心解码超参
PARAMETER temperature 0.6
PARAMETER top_p 0.95
PARAMETER repeat_penalty 1.15

# 3. 强力系统提示词：约束必须直接在 <think> 标签内进行深度反思，结束立刻给出最终结果
SYSTEM """
You are an expert autonomous reasoning AI. Think carefully through the problem step by step inside <think>...</think> tags.
Once reasoning is complete, provide the concise, direct, and actionable answer immediately without repeating reasoning steps.

T3 Code founder just shared his personal setup for building agentic teams with Grok Bot + Opus 5.5

one Grok Bot runs your whole fleet of machines. Opus 5.5 does the coding. you only approve

how:

→ Grok Bot gets one MCP link to T3 Code
→ you give it one rule: code goes to Opus 5.5
→ it spins up threads on every machine you own
→ works from your phone, even with the laptop closed

save the video, here's the guide:

• step 0 → what it is:

Grok Bot = always-on agent with its own cloud computer

T3 Code = open-source control plane for coding agents. free, runs on your machines, uses your subscriptions

• step 1 → the stack:

- Claude $100 plan → Opus 5.5 for the actual code
- Grok Bot → the dispatcher that never sleeps
- T3 Code on every box you want it to control

• step 2 → connect the fleet:

run npx t3 connect on each machine. one command, free, no Tailscale needed

• step 3 → give Grok Bot the keys:

Settings → Environments → Copy MCP URL → paste it into Grok Bot, sign in with OAuth. it can now see every linked machine

• step 4 → the one rule Theo uses:

tell Grok Bot "call T3 Code with Opus 5.5 for any task where it is applicable"

code runs on your Claude plan, Grok Bot's limits stay free for planning

• step 5 → make it work:

- "spin up an Opus 5.5 thread on each machine to check disk & RAM"
- "go through these PRs and pick the best ones"
- "split the backlog, one thread per issue, each in its own worktree"

every thread gets its own branch. nothing merges without your approval

what to expect:
- 8 threads on 8 machines from one chat (Theo's demo)
- works over the internet, not computer use
- control everything from your phone
- T3 Code: $0. you pay for Claude + Grok Bot only

honest take:

this is a dispatcher, not magic. bad briefs still give bad PRs, and you still review every diff. the win: your agents keep working while you're away from the desk

Save it so you don't lose it. 

then read the full guide on building AI agent teams in T3 Code in the article below ↓

viral_posts.full_text_en:
Claude without skills is a toy. I still don't get why everyone isn't using them.

I just added one free skill to my library and asked Claude Code for "a robot dragonfly, taken apart piece by piece."

Wings are where every 3D model I've tried turns to cardboard.

Top vs bottom:

> The top wings are 0.1 mm film with every vein showing through while the bottom ones are flat grey paddles.
> Each eye on top opens a 10-leaf shutter behind 40 mm of glass and the bottom eye is a painted ring.
> Every leg on top runs 2 servos down into a grip roller and the bottom legs are plain black sticks.
> The top chest opens on 3 spur gears and 11 pistons while the bottom one opens on a few grey blocks.
> At the breakdown the top one throws bolts, washers and gears into the air and the bottom one splits into a handful of chunks.
> Both rebuild and take off at 7.5 Hz but only the top one catches light like glass and metal.

The part that got me?

I used to think a better picture meant waiting for a better model. Turns out it meant handing the one I already have better instructions.

How the skill gets into Claude is below 👇
viral_posts.full_text_zh:
没有技能的克劳德就是一个玩具。我仍然不明白为什么每个人都不使用它们。

我刚刚在我的库中添加了一项免费技能，并向 Claude Code 询问“一只机器人蜻蜓，被一块一块地拆开”。

翅膀是我尝试过的每个 3D 模型都会变成纸板的地方。

顶部与底部：

> 顶部翅膀是 0.1 毫米薄膜，每条静脉都清晰可见，而底部翅膀是扁平的灰色桨。
> 顶部的每只眼睛在 40 毫米玻璃后面打开一个 10 叶快门，底部的眼睛是一个涂漆的环。
> 顶部的每条腿都将 2 个伺服系统向下运行到夹紧滚轮中，底部的腿是纯黑色的棍子。
> 顶部箱子打开后有 3 个正齿轮和 11 个活塞，而底部箱子打开后有几个灰色方块。
> 发生故障时，顶部的一个将螺栓、垫圈和齿轮抛向空中，底部的一个则分裂成几块。
> 两者都以 7.5 Hz 的频率重建和起飞，但只有顶部的一个能像玻璃和金属一样发光。

吸引我的部分？

我曾经认为更好的图片意味着等待更好的模型。事实证明，这意味着我已经有了更好的指示。
